narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low academic standing in law school was the dominant reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA also mattered, but they worked in the opposite direction. At 31, your LSAT was noticeably below the 37-point average of accepted students, and your 2.7 undergraduate GPA sat well under their 3.23 average. Even so, these two academic signals were not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your law-school class rankings.

Your family income bracket and plan to attend full-time were considered but had little effect on the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your class performance in the remaining law-school years, seek targeted bar-prep support, and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. A stronger academic record and higher test score would likely change the model’s prediction in a future application. (218 words)
